Product development boss at Marks & Spencer inspires niche outfits after unexpected success on social media

S he is not the most likely viral star. But with 310,000 followers on TikTok and 270,000 on Instagram, Marks & Spencer Food’s director of product development, Kathryn Turner, has suddenly become one of the year’s big hits on social media. Her videos take the viewer with her as she goes in-store to look at new dessert launches, including its banana, caramel and pecan pudding, or taste test its latest products, such as its cherry and chocolate cookies .

Turner is part of Marks & Spencer’s wider social media strategy implemented in 2020 as a way of attracting younger shoppers. Instead of using traditional influencers, M&S now champions 100 of its own employees on TikTok .

Turner, who launched her account in May, now regularly receives more than 1m likes on her videos, with celebrities including Nigella Lawson and Stormzy among her followers. Part of the appeal is Turner’s insider knowledge and expertise: she has worked at M&S since 1995.

This weekend, she will gain another prestigious accolade as fans spurn ghosts, witches and vampires and instead dress up as her for Halloween . The formula is simple. Some Turner-esque glasses, a blond wig and a packet of M&S cookies.

The content creator Liam Gleed has been posting videos of himself as Turner in the run-up to Halloween and plans to wear the costume this weekend. “To be very real, I love a sweet treat and I work close to an M&S so I follow her socials to find out what snacks I’ll be getting every Friday at work,” he says. “The more niche you go for Halloween, the better. Why go as basic characters when you can dress as your current fixation or icons of the internet?”

Gleed says it is the “real person” element that appeals to him. “I think it’s quite hilarious that someone who works as a product developer at M&S can become this on social media,” he says. “That’s what made the content work so well – it is so random that she is this popular figure from quite a normal job.”

Dressing like someone such as Turner – an improbable online star – rather than a spooky character or a movie star fits into the idea of Gay Halloween. This is a way of approaching the dress-up holiday that utilises an online pop culture reference – the more specific the better. It taps into “if you know, you know” culture.

This year, that could be anything from an iced coffee at a job interview, based on a viral story about whether or not it is acceptable, to Chappell Roan’s security guard, who allegedly made a fan cry , or the prenup papers for Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s marriage.

According to the website Know Your Meme , the term Gay Halloween dates to 2023 but had a precursor in “jokes about ‘Gay Halloween’ costumes being absurdly niche” on X. The idea has now spread to everyone online, however.

“I don’t think that gay people are exclusively culpable for this,” says James Greig, features editor of Dazed. “I can remember around 2016 finding it really annoying when straight guys were going [to Halloween parties] as very, very niche memes.”

It is well documented that Halloween has been embraced by queer people owing to the holiday providing the freedom to dress up without judgment – it is sometimes called “gay Christmas” – and Gleed argues that its origins remain here.

“Personally, as a gay man, I think it’s just another way for us to express ourselves,” he says. “We aren’t afraid to be our authentic selves after coming out, and to dress as someone so niche makes it comedic gold. I think the gays are doing it best because we don’t feel that shame of getting judged because we have been anyway.”

As for which Gay Halloween costumes may be popular this year, José Criales-Unzueta, style correspondent at Vanity Fair, wrote about the trend recently. They have a few predictions beyond Turner, including references to Heated Rivalry and Drake’s recent viral poncho.

The internet is also championing a New York pothole filled by the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani , and the foliage during Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl performance . “But the best ones are the ones you cannot foresee,” says Criales-Unzueta. “Part of the magic of Gay Halloween is the unexpected.”

items.lbText:
Caitlin Boswell of Tax Justice UK and others on what Aditya Chakrabortty described as a ‘Martin Lewis budget’

Aditya Chakrabortty was spot-on in his analysis of John Healey’s budget ( Burnham promised big change – where was it? Instead we got the Martin Lewis budget, 28 October ). It was a drop in the ocean of what is needed to bring about the scale of change this country needs and, importantly, was promised by Andy Burnham.

As the affordability crisis rages on, people may feel some relief at the small cost of living measures announced for households and businesses. But when we’ve been told we’ll get a wholesale reset and an end to neoliberalism, 4p off the price of gherkins and a temporary tiny bank tax isn’t going to cut it.

So, what’s the solution? The government must fairly tax the vast fortunes of the richest people and corporations, left mostly untouched. Recouping the massive wealth and profits siphoned off to shady tax havens each year, equalising how the tax system treats income from wealth and work, and building HMRC’s capacity to properly measure and collect tax from the very richest would raise tens of billions to help pay for targeted, meaningful cost of living support and Burnham’s ambitious plans to fix the housing crisis, fund social care and devolve power and wealth to every region.

Reforming capital gains tax – a proposal supported by members of his own party – would make things fairer and raise around £19.7bn a year, enough to build 90,000 new council homes (the number needed each year to end the housing crisis) and train 128,000 new NHS nurses .

This government cannot survive much longer on vibes alone, and Labour is already on its last chance. Burnham must use his 10-year plan and spending review to lay out a proper roadmap to genuinely improve lives and transform the country, otherwise he risks being remembered for gherkins, which isn’t much better than Liz Truss’s lettuce. Caitlin Boswell Deputy director, external affairs, Tax Justice UK

Aditya Chakrabortty is right to say that Andy Burnham’s grand rhetoric and romantic notions need to be translated into a bold programme of change. Unless this government tackles income and wealth inequality seriously, people’s anger will unceremoniously sweep it from office at the next election. Hugh Firth Newcastle upon Tyne

Living in a rented band B property, my “breathing space” was short-lived on budget day. The £100 energy payment announced by the chancellor will be entirely swallowed up by Northern Energy’s own announcement via email at 5pm the same day: “a temporary fuel surcharge of £17 per delivery will be applied to LPG deliveries as from your next delivery”.

Although this is “temporary”, customers are warned that the need to cover the elevated fuel costs is likely to remain for the foreseeable future. I had six deliveries of LPG last year – do the maths. Juliet Lunn Cockermouth, Cumbria

Once again, tax thresholds are frozen. What a missed opportunity. It would have been so easy to raise the threshold in line with the state pension, and keep them aligned. This simple mechanism would ensure that those with no other income pay no tax, and keep a little more money in the pockets of working people and others on very low incomes. Maybe next year? Jack Kenward South Molton, North Devon

Although abolishing the standing charge is something I agree with, presumably one of the groups that will benefit are second (and third) home owners. This includes approximately 177 MPs , Airbnb properties and holiday lets. John Victor Davies Hastings, East Sussex

I know that things are tight, but could the government not have funded a red box with “CR III” painted on it rather than the “ER II” sported by Mr Healey? Robert Bowden Bristol

Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday it is investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident “does look like a hack on Binance”.

It wasn’t immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to accomplish and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered, but stablecoin issuers quickly froze funds Thursday evening.

“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” a Binance spokesperson said in a statement.

“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement continued.

Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident.

Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen more than an equivalent of $800m in currency associated with the incident “in coordination with law enforcement”. The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday afternoon to under $79,000.

items.lbText:
With the chain on the brink of administration, its low-profile US owners face questions about their conduct

‘I t was a very successful and simple proposition,” laments one former Poundland boss. With every product in the shop sold at £1, and the price in its name, its proposition to shoppers was the clearest of any UK high street chain.

Now the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer could disappear amid heavy competition and inflation that has eaten into its ability to offer bargains.

Its potential collapse has brought distress for its up to 12,000 staff in the run-up to Christmas, and as shoppers head to the chain for Halloween costumes and treats.

Meanwhile, its low-profile owners are facing questions from the prime minister over their behaviour in the week his government’s budget attempted to offer support to the high street .

Poundland’s future hangs in the balance – and not for the first time – after the 36-year-old retailer filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court on Thursday, with the advisory firm AlixPartners lined up to run the process.

The legal measure protects Poundland, which operates 600 stores, including Dealz outlets in Ireland, from the demands of creditors for 10 days while a solution to its problems is sought. However, the prospect of it avoiding mass store closures and job losses diminishes by the day as suppliers hold back on deliveries, hurting its ability to trade.

The chain’s potential demise comes after Gordon Brothers, the American restructuring specialist which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from its previous owner in June last year, rejected a management-backed rescue bid for the whole chain by Martin Property Group.

While the Northern Irish firm is still in talks about taking on Poundland, it is understood its offer amounts to about £15m. That would pay off only half the £30m shareholder loan, the majority of which was taken on by Gordon Brothers when it bought the company. The deal would also include taking on a further, asset-backed loan worth about £90m, it is understood.

This deal has been rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, Poundland’s former owner, which holds the other £7.5m of the debt, being prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business, as first reported by Sky News.

One source who knows Poundland well said that Gordon Brothers had already taken about £10m in fees and interest out of the chain in the last year and that wanting another £30m was “egregious”. Gordon Brothers did not respond to a request for comment and has not confirmed this figure.

Gordon Brothers said earlier this week that options for the whole and parts of the business “are being thoroughly and objectively evaluated, with a view to minimising uncertainty for Poundland’s people and all relevant stakeholders”.

Sources close to the process said Gordon Brothers was unwilling to accept the Martin deal as the latest offer includes only about £7.5m up front and the rest over the next two years, leaving uncertainty for creditors, staff and suppliers.

One source said Gordon Brothers had sought bidders for the whole of Poundland but “the market had spoken” and only one little-known financial bidder with no history of running a large retail chain in the UK had come forward who might only go on to break up Poundland itself.

Instead, the restructuring specialist is understood to believe that suppliers and staff would be safer with the “trusted established retail operators” who have already put forward firm offers for parcels of outlets that amount to about half of Poundland’s stores, which could be converted to their formats.

A deal may yet be agreed with Martin over the next 10 days, especially with political pressure from Andy Burnham. On Friday, he told the Telegraph: “We want to see jobs protected. If there was a potential owner to avoid this that hasn’t been accepted, then the business secretary and I want to know why that is the case.”

For now, Gordon Brothers appears more keen on a break-up after losing faith in the likelihood of Poundland finding a route to long-term profitability amid tough times on the high street and heavy competition.

Rapid inflation on the cost of goods and labour, energy and business rates in recent years has forced Poundland to take a hit on profits and sell products for more than £1, including items for £5 or more.

In the past, Poundland removed products if it could not sell them profitably for a pound, but its choices have become more limited. High inflation – triggered first by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and then the Middle East conflict – has exposed a business model which always appeared to have a shelf life.

In most supermarkets a two-litre bottle of milk costs over £2, a pack of KitKats is at least £1.50 and a tin of Heinz baked beans is about £1.40, according to the price comparison site Trolley. Cutting the size of Poundland has, meanwhile, reduced its scale, making it harder to get good deals from suppliers to protect margins.

Poundland has also admitted that it made mistakes in recent years, including putting its Pepco clothing ranges into stores, which proved unpopular with UK shoppers.

The expansion of cut-price chains such as Savers, The Range, B&M, The Works and Home Bargains alongside budget online rivals such as Temu, Shein and Amazon means the cheaper end of the UK retail market is now very crowded.

Meanwhile, the low-wage shoppers that make up the core of Poundland’s clientele have little spare cash for non-essentials amid rising household bills . Those with more to spare have more options in their supermarket shop, where they are increasingly locked in by loyalty-card-linked discounts.…

items.lbText:
It was an ambitious notion – now Californians will vote on a one-time 5% billionaire tax, and state’s super rich have pulled out all the stops in opposition

One year ago, the idea of a billionaire tax in California was still in its infancy.

It wasn’t yet one of the most contentious ballot measure fights in state history – pitting Democrats against Democrats, drawing national attention from political heavyweights, and netting hundreds of millions of Silicon Valley dollars to fight it. Back then, it was a bold and desperate answer to Donald Trump’s healthcare cuts.

Trump had just signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which dictated a trillion dollars of Medicaid, Affordable Care Act and other healthcare funding be cut over the next decade to offset sweeping tax cuts. When the bill goes into effect in January, that could mean more than 3.4m Californians will lose their coverage, including millions of children.

“That’s why we were willing to do something that lots of people said was crazy,” said Dave Regan, the divisive architect of the billionaire tax and president of the healthcare union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW). “To us, what’s crazy is doing nothing and watching millions of people lose coverage.”

Now, with the midterms less than a week away, California voters will decide on whether to pass the ballot measure known as Proposition 40. The proposal would levy a one-time 5% tax on billionaires living in the state as of 1 January 2026, the proceeds of which would fund healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance.

The initiative has its critics, even among Democrats, who point at its structure as a one-off tax that would only fund certain healthcare programs. But its most vocal critics have been billionaires.

The idea of taxing the Golden State’s ultra-wealthy has snowballed into a messy brawl over the last year. Progressive politicians have become bedfellows with tech billionaires, opposition ballot measure campaigns have been mounted, Signal chats leaked, and boatloads of money have been spent.

Tech billionaires have treated the proposal as an existential threat, dumping upwards of $356m into “independent expenditure-only” political action committees (Super Pacs) to stop it. In the first two weeks of October, according to the most recent campaign filings, the opposition campaign spent more than $42.8m – surpassing $2.5m per day. That money went to an army of consultants , who have been tasked with lobbying politicians, blanketing the airwaves with ads and placing op-eds in Latino newspapers across the state.

“This looks like it’s going to be the most expensive ballot measure ever,” said David McCuan, a political science professor at Sonoma State University. “Not in California history, but in the history of the world.”

Meanwhile, the far-less-funded pro-Prop 40 camp has relied on viral social media campaigns from influencers and actors, including the artist Shepard Fairey and actor Mark Ruffalo , and raucous rallies headlined by leftwing politicians. During one packed event in San Francisco earlier this month, Vermont’s Bernie Sanders said: “The whole country, and frankly people from around the world, are paying attention to what is happening here.”

While Prop 40 is just one ballot measure election in one state, it is causing ripple effects nationwide. It comes at a time when affordability is top of mind and the disparity of wealth in the US hasn’t been so stark since the Great Depression . McCuan said the billionaires’ big spend was partially due to a fear of contagion to other states. Likewise, supporters say they hope the proposed tax is a harbinger for referendums on wealth inequality across the country.

Regan and his union got started on their endeavor last summer. After Trump signed his bill on 4 July, Regan’s team began making calls. They put together a working group of policy experts, economists, lawyers, researchers and political consultants, who came up with the one-time 5% tax to keep hospitals open and union healthcare workers in their jobs.

Regan is known for using the ballot measure process as a political tool to strongarm deals with lawmakers and push causes important to the SEIU-UHW. Since 2012, the union has sponsored 48 initiatives . The strategy with the billionaire tax was to sharpen the focus on inequality.

“We worked to come up with something that could draw enough support from voters, and that could avoid a catastrophe,” Regan said. “We just bore down on that.”

When their plan became public after the October 2025 filing deadline, the billionaires hatched a working group of their own.

Chris Larsen, a cryptocurrency mogul, hosted a Christmas party in northern California’s swanky Marin county last December, according to Bloomberg . It was in a treehouse tucked into a grove of towering redwood trees. The singer Janelle Monáe performed and California governor Gavin Newsom was there, along with Google co-founder Sergey Brin.

Newsom’s relationship with Brin goes back decades to when he was mayor of San Francisco. The governor, now a presumed presidential candidate, had flown on Google’s jet with Brin , and the two men attended each other’s weddings. But a lengthy exchange they reportedly had at Larsen’s party was far from collegial.

Brin confronted Newsom about the proposed billionaire tax, according to people who spoke with Newsom, Bloomberg reported. The Google co-founder, currently worth about $245bn, told the governor it was forcing him to leave California.

Newsom and Brin did not respond to the Guardian’s detailed list of questions.…

Housing secretary says Labour wants to reverse fortunes of towns plagued by boarded-up shops and rogue businesses

Angela Rayner has said voters will begin to see a difference in their high street before the next general election as Labour prioritises investment in struggling local communities.

The housing secretary said the government had made it a top priority before the country goes to the polls to begin turning around the fortunes of places blighted by boarded-up shops and rogue businesses.

“There’s been a real sense of decline,” she said. “People see it as part of the identity of their town and area, and that’s why we’ve got our high streets strategy.”

Speaking after John Healey, the chancellor, earmarked more than £1bn in his debut budget on Wednesday to support retail, hospitality and leisure businesses, Rayner signalled that the government stood ready to take further action.

“The chancellor has shown he’s backing our high streets, backing our businesses that have been struggling and giving them the breathing space,” she said. “And he’s going to continue with that.”

In an interview for the Guardian’s series on the fortunes of Britain’s towns, Rayner insisted that the budget was “moving the needle” for the economy as she sought to defend Healey from criticism.

On Thursday the chancellor was warned by the Resolution Foundation and the Institute for Fiscal Studies that his measures were poorly targeted and had paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year.

Meanwhile, the owners of Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators , putting up to 12,000 jobs at risk in a blow for towns across the country where the discount chain is a high street fixture.

Speaking before that announcement, Rayner said the government was taking action to ease the pressure on businesses and households amid the damage to Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.

“All these businesses that people value, that make up a thriving high street, the chancellor is really giving them support,” she said.

Asked whether voters would be able to see a difference in their local shopping districts before the next general election, she said: “The money will start to come through. Already we’ve put the £5.8bn in.

“Next year, from April, business rates [cuts] will apply and you’ll see [other] money in more areas.”

On his way to becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged a new dawn for Britain’s high streets , placing the revival of overlooked town centres at the heart of his agenda for government.

In response to this agenda, Healey said he would cut business rates for retail, hospitality and leisure companies in a plan worth £1bn over two years, with the relief partly funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops.

Labour also launched a revamped “hope on the high street” strategy alongside the chancellor’s budget to coordinate investment and the transfer of power to local leaders. This includes the already announced £5.8bn “pride in place” programme to support regeneration projects and £210m fund to transform derelict buildings .

“There’s a lot of money and funding pots going into the high street, as well as work in the public realm to deliver services and housing,” Rayner said.

However, business leaders said more fundamental changes to the business rates system were needed, highlighting that Labour had promised to replace it entirely in its manifesto.

Before the budget Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, told the Guardian that changes to tax online sales at higher rates than in-store purchases were needed to help “level the playing field” for struggling bricks-and-mortar stores.

Hinting at further changes to come, budget documents show ministers are exploring “how the business rates system could better target online retailers in ways that minimise any indirect impacts for wider retail businesses” to fund support for the high street.

items.lbText:
After UK’s hottest summer on record, Ardingly near Haywards Heath is just 19% full – and next-closest reservoir is unusable due to broken treatment works

“Y ou can see the water level at Ardingly going down and down. I don’t remember ever seeing it this low,” says Caroline Allan, a lifetime resident of Haywards Heath, the nearest town to one of England’s most depleted reservoirs.

The Ardingly reservoir, managed by South East Water and serving about 95,000 properties in and around Haywards Heath and Uckfield in Sussex, is currently 19% full.

The day the Guardian visited, the weather was grey and rainy, incongruous with the muddy reservoir bed that should have been submerged under six metres of water.

Earlier this month a severe drought was declared in parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex, with urgent measures being taken to secure public water supplies after the UK experienced its hottest summer on record .

Severe drought is the highest level of drought and is declared when evidence shows drought is causing or will soon cause serious harm, and when emergency action is needed to protect people, water supplies, the environment, farming, infrastructure or other critical services.

“They will probably never lift the hosepipe ban and it just seems so unfair that they’re making the area more and more crowded but they’re not increasing the capacity to store water,” said Allan.

There has been a steady stream of new housing developments around Haywards Heath, sparking local opposition , with concerns that a growing local population is putting pressure on already strained resources.

Water demand is increasing as the population grows and new industrial demands from datacentres and energy infrastructure require more water. Plus, the water available to supply those needs is reducing as the climate crisis worsens, resulting in greater variability and unpredictability of rainfall and greater water demand during hotter, drier summers. There has also been a lack of investment over several decades in fixing leaks and building new reservoirs.

Most of Europe has endured back-to-back climate crisis-driven heatwaves this summer. The extreme heat, coupled with little rainfall, means 82% of England and large parts of Wales are still in drought or severe drought.

The Environment Agency would expect reservoir storage to be about 75% at this time of year and yet supplies at several reservoirs are critically low. This includes Ardingly and Wimbleball, which supplies South West Water customers and is 14.5% full.

It is estimated that 120% of average rainfall is needed between now and April for all areas to be considered out of drought. The government’s national drought group was told on Wednesday that despite the “weather whiplash” brought by Storm Austen and Boelo , the recent rain has not changed the drought outlook.

Less than six miles away from Ardingly, Southern Water’s Weir Wood reservoir is 80% full because a water treatment works at the site has been out of action since 2018.

“It’s crazy that they’ve got Weir Wood next door and they’re not using it. I think that’s madness,” Allan said.

Graham Ward, who has lived in Haywards Heath for his whole life, also said it was “crazy” that there was a full neighbouring reservoir that cannot be used.

During the drought in 2025, South East Water announced emergency plans to connect the Ardingly and Weir Wood reservoirs together by an overground pipeline. When the rain came and the drought conditions eased, these plans were shelved.

Southern Water is now seeking to rebuild the treatment works at Weir Wood by 2030, and South East Water is conducting a feasibility study of a buried pipeline to connect the two reservoirs.

But after government guidance to stockpile essential goods , water scarcity has become a pressing concern for local residents. “We’re really not that far away from Weir Wood, and we’ve got Ardingly with hardly any water in it and we’re told to buy water. It’s just crazy,” said Allan.

Ward said he has already been storing water for some time in anticipation.

“I am worried, but I also think there should be responsibility on the water companies to get the reservoirs working as they should be. The infrastructure is crumbling and it’s not fit for purpose any more; if we continually have hot summers, this is going to be a problem every year,” he said.

Delphine Hazeldon, who has lived in Haywards Heath for more than 20 years, also said she has never seen the Ardingly reservoir so low.

“Our relatives in Australia, they’re always asking for updates and they’re horrified. It is a definite worry, we’re approaching 80, but we think well, it’ll be our children and our children’s children facing the problem. The whole thing is a mess.”

A spokesperson at Southern Water said: “Weir Wood reservoir is being rebuilt to ensure long-term water resilience for the North Sussex region, in the face of climate change and population growth. The existing treatment works date from the 1950s and reached the end of its operational life, with significant reliability and water-quality challenges. The site was therefore taken out of supply in 2018. “While a number of options were considered, a complete rebuild was identified as the best long-term solution to provide a reliable and resilient water supply for customers in the area. While we already supply water to South East Water through an existing interconnected network, Ardingly’s current situation would not be resolved if Weir Wood treatment works were operational.”

Water minister, Emma Hardy, who chaired a national drought group meeting on Wednesday, said: “Despite the recent rain, the situation remains serious. As we move through autumn and winter, we now face the challenge of having drought and flood simultaneously as the rain struggles to be absorbed by the hardened ground.…

items.lbText:
As thousands of datacentres are constructed across Europe, the Guardian and Investigate Europe have uncovered disturbing evidence that some workers building them are exposed to dangerous conditions and living in fear of speaking out

S andu* checked his watch. He was winding down the last 15 minutes of his shift at a vast Google datacentre site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium, in March, when the call came in. The 34-year-old electrical tester had already worked almost 10 hours, but says such last-minute jobs were normal: “I had no choice. People have been fired after saying no.”

The task was one Sandu had done many times before and involved a series of tests measuring the safety and integrity of the electrical wiring. A protective suit was locked away in an equipment room. The round trip would have added another 15 minutes to the job, he says, and people were waiting, so he decided not to retrieve the suit.

Once in the voltage room, Sandu says the managers confirmed the lines had been de-energised. In the first round, everything went as planned. Then, on the second test, while holding insulated tongs, he linked the cables. But this time, the lines were live.

The blast was immediate and catastrophic. In milliseconds, 400 volts and 12,000 amps hit Sandu’s face and across the right side of his body. “I went completely blind,” he says. When doctors received him in the Grand Hôpital de Charleroi, he says he was placed in an induced coma for five days.

Hospital records seen by the Guardian and Investigate Europe show that the arc flash electrocution had burned 12% of Sandu’s body, with second-degree burns to the face and neck, as well as third-degree burns across his right shoulder and fingers.

When Sandu woke from surgery in the intensive care unit a week later, his wife was at his bedside. He says his entire body felt like a “white-hot blister … It was so much pain. The human heart cannot comprehend it.”

Sandu says the regional director of Google, along with a representative from Dornan Engineering, an Irish company that oversaw his contractor, and his recruiter, came to visit. While he lay bandaged in the hospital bed, he says the Google director told him he was lucky to be alive.

To date, no company or contractor appears to have been found liable for the accident. The local labour inspectorate closed its investigation in late October and found no wrongdoing.

A spokesperson for Dornan Engineering said it was “committed to maintaining safe working conditions, complying with applicable labour laws and continually learning to help prevent incidents like this from happening again”.

Sandu’s electrocution appears brutal and harrowing, but far from unique, according to a five-month investigation by Investigate Europe and the Guardian into conditions for migrant workers on datacentre sites across Sweden , Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands.

Europe is in the midst of a datacentre boom, the largest infrastructure surge the continent has seen in decades, with more than 2,300 datacentres rapidly altering the physical and energy landscape of Europe (at least 500 of them in the UK) and hundreds more under construction. But unions say the push for tech sovereignty in Europe is becoming increasingly reliant on the exploitation of migrant workers.

In dozens of interviews we found evidence of debilitating injuries, squalid living conditions, an unreported infectious outbreak, unpaid wages and exploitative employment practices.

In the UK, a general contractor died while working on a datacentre site last year, while another fatality was reported in 2024 at an electrical substation being built for a Microsoft datacentre. Serious accidents have also been recorded this year at projects in Italy , Sweden , Norway and Belgium , and exploitative labour practices have been found at projects around the world, including in Brazil .

O n the outskirts of Gävle, a city two hours north of Stockholm, past timber-framed cottages and dense pine forests, lies a smooth road leading to one such site. The remote clearing is part of a 130-hectare, €3bn expansion plan begun in June 2024 to scale up Microsoft’s AI datacentre infrastructure.

One subcontractor at the site is the Irish-owned construction company BenBau. It is among 148 firms working under Collen Construction at the Gävle site, including 28 direct subcontractors.

For months, there has been a growing sense of outrage among Adrian*, 45, and his colleagues working for BenBau on the Microsoft site. They showed evidence of crowded living quarters – 24 people to a kitchen, 14 men to a single bathroom – and say they have reported vermin infestations, broken ventilation systems and lack of heating during the sub-zero Swedish winters, but the problems remain.

Such conditions can make the transmission of disease more likely. In February this year, one Romanian worker tested positive for active tuberculosis, medical records show. Shortly after, others living in the same shared housing showed similar symptoms. BenBau initially informed only a few men who shared close quarters with the infected worker and then told the men that testing was optional, according to workers. After the first worker who contracted the disease had left for hospital, Benbau moved another worker into his bedroom.

Freedom of information requests made to Sweden’s national work authorities and its Public Health Agency say no outbreak had been reported.

The living and working conditions form only part of the story. More than 30 workers have shown hundreds of payslips to the Guardian and Investigate Europe that appear to show some of them working up to 50 or 60 hours a week with no overtime pay and missed holiday pay. With many foreign workers unfamiliar with the laws, unions say inequity can arise quickly.…

items.lbText:
John Healey has hit adult gaming centres with 25% tax. Undercover footage shows how they lure customers

The last of five £20 notes disappears into the slot machine as The Verve’s Bittersweet Symphony plays over the shop’s sound system.

That’s it, £100 gone in the space of about five minutes, swallowed up by one of the many “slot farms” that dominate the shopping streets of Peterborough .

All that’s left to show for it is a free KitKat, one of the incentives staff use to tempt customers into staying a little longer and losing a little more.

It’s lunchtime on a Thursday and dozens of glassy-eyed hopefuls are having the same experience, feeding in what little cash they have and cursing as it disappears.

The same pattern is repeated across the country. Gamblers in Great Britain lost £2.7bn on slot machines last year, nearly double the annual budget of the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, which oversees the sector.

In his inaugural budget this week, the chancellor, John Healey, took direct aim at slot machines by raising “machine games duty”, the tax levied on them, from 20% to 25%. This, he said, would bring in nearly £150m a year, “raising taxes on gambling to support good growth on every high street”.

But what is the reality of Britain’s booming slot machine industry and why is it in the government’s crosshairs?

That’s one reason why each machine earns £40,000 a year on average, more than the median pay of a British worker. Slot machines are found in bookmakers, casinos and bingo halls but the venues that really pack them are adult gaming centres (AGCs), sometimes known as slot farms.

They’re on pretty much every British high street, disproportionately in poorer areas . On some, such as this stretch in Peterborough, almost every shop is a bookmaker or an AGC.

By far the two biggest AGC operators are Admiral, which is owned by an Austrian billionaire, and Merkur, owned by a German billionaire. Both have targeted the UK for growth in recent years.

AGCs have their critics, including Andy Burnham, who has accused them of “ targeting some of the most vulnerable in our communities”. Notable examples include when Merkur was fined £100,000 in 2025, after the Guardian revealed it had allowed an older woman with terminal cancer to rack up huge losses over two spells lasting 16 hours.

As well as the potential for rapid losses, the machines are associated with higher rates of problem gambling than products such as sports betting. Critics also point to practices apparently designed to keep punters playing and losing. For a start, the majority of venues are open 24 hours a day , while the Guardian has previously revealed that staff are paid bonuses linked to customers’ losses , undermining their incentive to intervene to prevent problem gambling.

Shops are increasingly offering a new breed of super slot machine, featuring a comfy armchair and a highly-immersive, 65-inch screen. Staff will offer drinks and snacks to keep punters playing, there are regular prize draws and “free spin” offers, and you can make cash withdrawals from your bank without leaving the shop.

Punters will sometimes play more than one machine simultaneously. Admiral has introduced a two-machine limit, which it says is designed to reduce harmful gambling.

Many are open under bingo licences, which may sound more benign to local authority planning committees. In practice, most have one bingo machine that is rarely used, if ever.

On a one-off basis, it’s possible to win up to £500. In tests across several AGC venues, the Guardian occasionally won some money, which will be donated to charity. But the machines have a fixed “return to player”, meaning that regular slot machine players will always lose. That’s why slots are a good target for a tax raid, and a valuable cash cow for companies, which like predictable sources of income. It’s also why gambling harm experts think they’re dangerous.

Bookmakers say it will cost them money, leading to shop closures. Entain, which owns Ladbrokes, expects a £25m hit. But shares in the three listed slot machine operators – Entain, the William Hill owner Evoke and the Grosvenor Casinos owner Rank Group – rose sharply after the budget. Relieved investors had feared Healey would opt for a 40% rate.

AGCs were singled out by the chancellor, who said they and vape shops would be excluded from business rates relief, costing them a combined £10m. But AGCs appear well-placed to thrive anyway because of their low overheads and 24-hour opening. For the slot farms, it’s business as usual.

Neither Admiral nor Merkur responded to a request for comment. Bacta, the slot machine trade body, said its members’ venues were “among the safest places to gamble, with experienced staff on hand to identify problems and provide support to customers”.

“Player protection is central to our approach, and machines in AGCs are designed with inbuilt tools to encourage safe play, facilitate self-exclusion and help prevent problem gambling,” it said.

“Games in these venues are low-stake – costing as little as 10p a spin – and these businesses have been a longstanding part of the high street for decades, providing low-stake entertainment, local jobs and a boost to local economies. AGCs tend to open on high streets where there is already footfall, alongside other hospitality and leisure venues, and where planning and licensing permissions allow.

“Our members operate within one of the most tightly regulated licensing regimes in the world. Venues are regularly inspected, must comply with strict conditions, and can have licences refused or revoked where licensing objectives are at risk.”

Chancellor’s ‘new course’ includes a £100 one-off payment, low-carbon upgrade loans and an end to standing charges

John Healey has unveiled a package of support for households being buffeted by “global economic storms”.

“I’m setting a new course to get energy costs down in line with Europe,” the chancellor said in his maiden budget. In the long term, he hopes that changes in how Britain covers the cost of renewables and grid upgrades will “drive down all aspects of energy bills”.

British households face some of the highest energy charges for three years, with the war in the Middle East driving up oil and gas prices.

Under the government’s price cap, average dual-fuel bills are £1,700 a year and could rise to more than £2,100 a year from January, according to industry forecasts .

So what has the chancellor offered hard-pressed households to help them through the coldest months of the year? And will it be enough to lower gas and electricity bills?

This measure will offer a modest saving for most British households – but not all, and perhaps not until next winter.

Healey promised to end “unfair and outdated” standing charges on gas bills for 23m homes “in 2027 or as soon as possible after”. This could help almost two-thirds of households to save an average of £45 a year.

A standing charge is a fixed daily fee paid through all household gas bills, regardless of how much is used. It means homes that severely ration their gas use – or use none at all – still shoulder the same cost as a high-income household.

The charge typically adds about £100 a year to bills and the change means these costs will soon be recovered through a higher unit price for gas. For those with below-average gas use, bills should fall. But there won’t be savings for everyone.

Jonny Marshall, an economist at the Resolution Foundation, said households with high gas use might have higher bills when the unit rate increases. These could include low-income households who have bigger families or poorly insulated homes.

A home using 7,000 kilowatt hours of gas a year would save about £40 under the change, but a household using 14,000 kWh of gas a year could be £25 worse off, according to Richard Neudegg, a director at Uswitch.com. A household using the typical 11,500 kWh shouldn’t see any change, he added.

The government has already begun taking aim at taxes and policy costs loaded on to electricity bills that could over time mean removing hundreds of pounds from bills.

This month, it removed the 5% VAT levy on electricity bills for 29m households, effectively saving them about £45 a year.

This was supposed to help households through the coldest months of the year, until March. But Healey has promised to keep VAT off bills until July, extending the annual savings to £50 a year, according to the Treasury.

The move follows a string of cuts to electricity levies over the past year which have shaved about £150 a year off costs.

“For many years, under Conservative governments, policy costs were simply loaded on to household bills through levies,” Healey said. “Today, I am putting an end to that. We’ll introduce a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills.”

Healey confirmed he would consider steps to remove standing charges on electricity too, which ​add about £200 a year to the average ​bill. The savings from this measure remain unclear, depending on which costs would move into general taxation and which would be covered through the unit price for electricity.

Healey will continue to alter a subsidy scheme for the UK’s oldest renewable energy projects, around three-quarters of which has been removed from bills and covered by general taxation. The research charity Nesta said this would lower electricity costs by £42 a year.

Healey has scrapped plans for a levy to support hydrogen projects that would otherwise have added £2.60 to £4.50 a year to the average dual-fuel bill.

The government believes that households could save up to £550 a year on energy bills if they invest in solar panels, home batteries and a heat pump. These savings could rise by a further £300 a year with a time-of-use tariff, according to the government.

To help households access these savings, a Warm Home Loans scheme, which launched on Tuesday, will offer government-backed loans of up to £35,000 for low-carbon energy alternatives.

The government said it was committed to rolling out heat pumps through its boiler upgrade scheme, which provides grants of up to £7,500 to help meet the £13,600 cost of installing one.

Grants of up to £9,000 a year are available to households that are not connected to the gas grid and rely on high-cost heating oil.

For many, the government’s new measures will come too late to help this winter. But there could be support in the spring from a debt relief scheme.

The government said the delayed scheme will “provide targeted support to customers in genuine financial need”. Total household energy debt has tripled from 2021 to a record £5bn and could reach £7bn by the end of the year .

The one-off, targeted intervention has been designed to help those with debts from the 2022-24 energy crisis and little prospect of repaying them.

Nesta has suggested debt relief could be given to about 2m households for a one-off cost of £2.7bn. This would also cut the £29 a year paid by all households to cover the cost of unpaid bills.

More details on the scheme will follow in early 2027, the government said.
